news.content: Skip to main navigation Login Logout SUBSCRIBE Sign up for FREE daily enews × Menu Magazine Profiles in Business Giving Guide Digital Archives News People In The News Company Database Contact Us Advertise All Events Special Events -A +A Wildlife vaccine drop planned for August to help slow spread of rabies Opens in a new window Opens in a new window Opens in a new window Submitted by tim on Tue, 07/28/2026 - 05:17 Vermont Business Magazine The annual rabies vaccine bait drop will begin on Aug. 1 to continue combating rising rabies rates in Vermont wildlife. The U.S. Department of Agriculture’s Wildlife Services, in coordination with the Vermont departments of Health and Fish & Wildlife, will conduct the drops. The August rabies bait distribution will deliver approximately 915,700 rabies vaccine baits in areas of Addison, Caledonia, Chittenden, Essex, Franklin, Grand Isle, Lamoille, Orange, Orleans and Washington Counties, as well as parts of New York and New Hampshire. “Vaccinating wildlife against rabies remains an important tool to help protect people and animals, and slow the spread of rabies in Vermont,” said Natalie Kwit, DVM, state public health veterinarian with the Health Department. Rabies activity has risen sharply in recent years, with 66 rabid animals reported in both 2024 and 2025 – more than double the previous 10-year annual average number of cases. So far this year, 36 rabies cases have been reported – including 15 raccoons, nine skunks, eight bats and three foxes. Nearly every county in Vermont has been affected, with many cases concentrated in Orleans County. Officials are working to understand why more animals are testing positive for rabies, and surveillance efforts to monitor the increase are ongoing. Over the next month, baited vaccine – in the form of a sweet-smelling oral bait that is attractive for raccoons and skunks to eat – will be distributed across 10 counties by airplane in rural areas, helicopter in suburban areas, and by hand in residential areas. Find more information, including a full list of towns where bait will be distributed, on the Rabies Vaccine Bait Drop Fact Sheet on the Health Department’s website. Rabies is a viral disease that is deadly if people don't receive medical care before symptoms start. It is primarily spread through the bite of an infected animal. In Vermont, the disease is most often detected in raccoons, skunks, foxes, bats and woodchucks – but pets and livestock can also get rabies if they have not been vaccinated. Human rabies cases in the U.S. are most commonly caused by contact with bats. How to protect yourself and your pets: If you are bitten by an animal, wash the wound well with soap and water and contact your health care provider. Do not touch or handle wild or stray animals, even young ones. Learn more about what to do when you encounter a wild animal from the Department of Fish and Wildlife. Call the Vermont Rabies Hotline (1-800-4-RABIES) if you see a sick or strangely behaving animal, are bitten by a wild animal, or wake up to a bat in your sleeping area. Contact local law enforcement regarding concerns about stray pets. Make sure pets and livestock are up to date on vaccination. Keep pets indoors at night and supervise them when outside. During the rabies bait drop, leave vaccine baits where they are and call the Rabies Hotline if a pet or child eats or brings one home. Learn more about rabies in Vermont – visit www.HealthVermont.gov/rabies. news.title_zh: 野生动物 疫苗 计划于 8 月投放,以帮助减缓 狂犬病 的传播 - 佛蒙特州商业杂志
news.source_body_en: Vermont will begin its annual rabies vaccine bait drop on August 1, 2026, to combat rising rabies rates in wildlife. The Department of Agriculture’s Wildlife Services, in coordination with the Vermont departments of Health and Fish & Wildlife, will distribute approximately 915,700 vaccine baits across 10 Vermont counties, as well as parts of New York and New Hampshire. Rabies activity has surged, with 66 cases reported in both 2024 and 2025—more than double the previous decade's average—and 36 cases already in 2026. Nearly every Vermont county has been affected, with Orleans County seeing high concentrations. The oral vaccine baits, attractive to raccoons and skunks, will be deployed by airplane in rural areas, helicopter in suburban areas, and by hand in residential areas. Officials continue surveillance to understand the increase, while the public is urged to report concerns via the Vermont Rabies Hotline and ensure pets are vaccinated.

news.content: Skip to content Advertise News Business Opinion Education Lifestyle Sports Cities Avondale Estates Brookhaven Chamblee Clarkston Countywide Decatur Doraville Dunwoody Ellenwood Lithonia Pine Lake Stone Mountain Stonecrest Tucker Contact Us Legal Advertising Dept LOCATIONS Subscribe News Second bat tests positive for rabies this summer July 27, 2026 Christine Fonville A second case of rabies this summer in a bat has been confirmed by DeKalb County Animal Control (DCAES). On July 21, officials stated that a dead bat tested positive for rabies in south DeKalb near Columbia Drive and York Place. Early in July, a bat found near a neighborhood in Stone Mountain also tested positive for rabies after being found dead near Millstone Trail. While multiple mammals can carry and contract rabies, officials with Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) state that bats are the leading source of rabies in the U.S., and their teeth are so tiny that a bite or scratch can go unnoticed. “Avoid touching bats and seek a medical professional if you may have come into contact with one,” the CDC’s website states. “Rabies is a disease that affects the brain, and it is usually passed from animal to animal, but can be passed from animals to people,” said officials with DCAES. “The virus is spread through saliva, usually from a bite of an animal that has the disease.” According to the American Veterinary Medical Association, “Animals with rabies may show a variety of signs, including fearfulness, aggression, excessive drooling, difficulty swallowing, staggering, paralysis, and seizures. Aggressive behavior is common, but rabid animals may also be uncharacteristically affectionate. Rabid wild animals may lose their natural fear of humans and display unusual behavior; for example, an animal that is usually only seen at night may be seen wandering in the daytime.” There is no treatment once the clinical signs of rabies appear, stated the American Veterinary Medical Association’s website. People who are exposed to rabies through an animal exposure can be treated with “vaccines that provide immunity to rabies when administered soon after an exposure,” according to the Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine. The vaccines must be administered before symptoms of the disease are present to be effective, stated officials. “Georgia is a rabies endemic state, and the virus is present all year long,” said DCAES officials. “It is not unusual for the county to report several rabies cases each year.” Residents should make sure pets are up to date for preventative vaccination through their veterinarian and should eliminate outdoor feeding stations and access to garbage cans, said officials. Additionally, residents are advised to watch pets and contact DeKalb County Animal Control if unusual behavior occurs. “Vaccinations are effective in protecting humans and pets from the virus,” stated officials. “Residents are responsible for vaccinating pets every year and registering the tag with DeKalb County Animal Control.” For more information or to report any animal bite, contact DeKalb County Animal Control at 404-294-2996, from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m., Monday through Friday, or 404-294-2519 after hours. This latest case in south DeKalb marks the fourth time this year that DCAES officials have announced an animal was found to test positive for rabies. After 22 Oregon bats have tested positive for rabies in 2026, Oregon Health Authority and the Oregon Department of Fish and Wildlife are reminding people how to prevent exposure risk. The primary way people can stay safe is to not touch dead or dying animals, officials said. Also, to keep pets away. Oregon has matched its record for bats that tested positive for rabies in a year, OHA said. Bats are the primary animal to expose humans to the virus in the U.S. Bats rank second behind skunks in animals that have tested positive for rabies in Larimer County in recent years. 636525557169345144 Bat Though people might want to help a dead or dying bat, more contact with bats increased rabies exposure risk, OHA's Public Health Division veterinarian Emilio DeBess said. Advertisement Advertisement "When a bat or other wild animal is sick or dying with rabies, there's an increased chance they will bite or transmit the virus in other ways," DeBess said. Bats and other wildlife rarely bite people, but might if they are sick or threatened, ODFW state wildlife veterinarian Colin Gillin said. "Bats provide important ecosystem services in Oregon, but also globally with insect control, seed dispersal, and pollination of specific plants, supporting agriculture and forest systems," Gillin said. "And like many animals that can carry disease, bats can also prevent or suppress disease by reducing mosquitoes and other vectors that carry human and animal pathogens." What to do if you come across a bat Since bats are protected wildlife, and it is illegal to harm or keep them. ODFW and OHA provided the following list of tips if you see a sick bat: Advertisement Advertisement Stay calm, do not touch it. Keep people and pets away. If the sick or dead bat is indoors, do not release it. It may have exposed someone or a pet to rabies. Place a container or box over the bat if it's safe. If the sick or dead bat is outdoors and may have exposed someone to rabies, cover it with a box or bucket to keep it in place. But, leave the bat alone unless someone was bitten or scratched before it died. Immediately report if a person or pet has been bitten or scratched by an animal that may have rabies to local animal regulation services or local public health authority. Seek medical care immediately from a medical provider or veterinarian. If multiple sick or dead bats are observed in an area report to ODFW. Avoid bats seen in the wild, such as while hiking. Teach children to avoid all contact with bats and other wildlife. Update dog or cat vaccinations, whether they are indoor or outdoor pets. Unvaccinated pets that come into contact with a bat may be quarantined for up to four months, or euthanized. Protect your home from bats by covering vents, chimneys, and other entry points with screens. If roosting bats are living in the attic, call a wildlife control operator, not ODFW. More information about rabies and bats is avaliable at OHA's bats and rabies website and ODFW's bats website. Makenzie Stamets is an outdoor intern at the Statesman Journal. She can be reached at mstamets@statesmanjournal.com or on X at @MakenzieStamets. news.source_body_en: Oregon has matched its record for bats testing positive with rabies in 2026, with 22 cases confirmed by the Oregon Health Authority and the Oregon Department of Fish and Wildlife. Bats are the primary animal to expose humans to rabies in the U.S., and officials are urging residents to avoid contact with dead or dying bats to prevent transmission. The virus can spread through bites or scratches from infected bats, posing a risk to both humans and pets. Public health guidelines include reporting exposures, seeking immediate medical care, and ensuring pets are vaccinated. Unvaccinated pets exposed to bats may face quarantine or euthanasia. Authorities emphasize the importance of wildlife protection while minimizing rabies risks.

analysis.brief_en: The Vermont Department of Health has announced the start of the second round of rabies vaccine bait distribution for wildlife beginning August 1, 2026. This preventive measure aims to control rabies in animal populations across the state. The program follows established protocols for wildlife vaccination, with no specific case counts or risk levels provided in the announcement. The initiative represents a routine public health response to mitigate rabies transmission among wildlife, with no immediate threats to human health indicated.

analysis.brief_en: In St. Lawrence County, New York, authorities have confirmed a case of rabies in a raccoon, prompting the USDA Wildlife Services to conduct an aerial vaccine bait distribution this week. This initiative is part of a broader, nationwide cooperative effort to prevent rabies transmission, a disease fatal to both animals and humans. The targeted vaccine drop aims to immunize wildlife populations, particularly raccoons, to curb the spread of the virus. The operation underscores ongoing public health measures to manage rabies risks in rural and suburban areas where wildlife-human interactions are common.

news.content: × Web Image Sort by Relevance Date Home News Local News Booking Report Letters to the Editor Obituaries California U.S. & World Politics Advertising Specials Senior News Fire Call Log Fire News Advertise Contact Us Discover more Vehicle & Traffic Safety pet Demographics Merced County Sheriff's Animal Services Bureau Offer Safety Tips to Prevent Rabies Exposure and Keep Family and Pets Safe Details Last Updated: Wednesday, 29 July 2026 03:40 Published: Wednesday, 29 July 2026 05:02 Rabies Awareness: Avoid Contact with Bats July 29, 2026 – Merced County Sheriff's Animal Services Bureau officials remind the public about the dangers of rabies. Bats are an important part of our ecosystem, but some can carry rabies. Rabies is spread through the saliva of an infected animal, usually through a bite. While human rabies cases are rare, the disease is almost always fatal once symptoms develop. Prompt medical evaluation after a potential exposure can prevent rabies from developing. If you encounter a bat: - Do not touch or handle it, even if it appears sick, injured, or unable to fly. - Keep children and pets away. - If a bat is found inside your home, close the door to the room if possible and contact a licensed wildlife exclusion or pest control professional for assistance. - If you, a family member, or your pet may have had contact with a bat—even if you are unsure whether a bite occurred—contact your healthcare provider, veterinarian, or local Animal Services as soon as possible. Bat bites can be small and difficult to detect. Discover more Occupational Health & Safety Wildlife News California law requires dogs to be vaccinated against rabies, and rabies vaccination is strongly recommended for cats. Keeping pets current on their rabies vaccinations is the best way to protect them if they come into contact with wildlife. Simple precautions can help protect you, your family, and your pets while allowing bats to continue their important role in our environment. news.content_original: × Web Image Sort by Relevance Date Home News Local News Booking Report Letters to the Editor Obituaries California U.S. & World Politics Advertising Specials Senior News Fire Call Log Fire News Advertise Contact Us Discover more Vehicle & Traffic Safety pet Demographics Merced County Sheriff's Animal Services Bureau Offer Safety Tips to Prevent Rabies Exposure and Keep Family and Pets Safe Details Last Updated: Wednesday, 29 July 2026 03:40 Published: Wednesday, 29 July 2026 05:02 Rabies Awareness: Avoid Contact with Bats July 29, 2026 – Merced County Sheriff's Animal Services Bureau officials remind the public about the dangers of rabies. Bats are an important part of our ecosystem, but some can carry rabies. Rabies is spread through the saliva of an infected animal, usually through a bite. While human rabies cases are rare, the disease is almost always fatal once symptoms develop. Prompt medical evaluation after a potential exposure can prevent rabies from developing. If you encounter a bat: - Do not touch or handle it, even if it appears sick, injured, or unable to fly. - Keep children and pets away. - If a bat is found inside your home, close the door to the room if possible and contact a licensed wildlife exclusion or pest control professional for assistance. - If you, a family member, or your pet may have had contact with a bat—even if you are unsure whether a bite occurred—contact your healthcare provider, veterinarian, or local Animal Services as soon as possible. Bat bites can be small and difficult to detect. Discover more Occupational Health & Safety Wildlife News California law requires dogs to be vaccinated against rabies, and rabies vaccination is strongly recommended for cats. Keeping pets current on their rabies vaccinations is the best way to protect them if they come into contact with wildlife. Simple precautions can help protect you, your family, and your pets while allowing bats to continue their important role in our environment. news.content: 24/7 LivePhiladelphiaPennsylvaniaNew JerseyDelaware 89° Raccoons 2nd raccoon sought after rabies-positive animal attacks South Jersey man By6abc Digital Staff and Caroline Goggin Thursday, July 30, 2026 3:35AM 2nd raccoon sought after rabies-positive animal attacks NJ man GLASSBORO, N.J. (WPVI) -- Gloucester County officials are searching for a raccoon after another animal involved in an encounter tested positive for rabies. The investigation stems from an attack Sunday morning outside the Glassboro home of Kevin Tucker. "I was walking to leave when a raccoon came out of the shrubbery and charged me," Tucker said. "I kind of fell backward, and I think that's when it bit the front part of my right leg." READ MORE | Man recalls raccoon attack outside NJ home: 'I could see these bright yellow eyes' The raccoon was eventually captured in Anthony Alvarado's backyard - just steps from where Tucker was bitten. "It was running around making weird noises," Alvarado told Action News. "It was actually kind of foaming at the mouth a bit, so that's how I knew it had rabies." Officials said the raccoon that attacked Tucker has since tested positive for rabies. Authorities also said the infected animal had been seen fighting with another raccoon before its capture. Efforts are now underway to locate that second raccoon. Action News returned to the neighborhood on Wednesday afternoon to speak with Tucker, who said he is now on high alert. "I just don't know what might pop out of where and when," he said. He has spent the past few days fielding phone calls from the Gloucester County Health Department and Gloucester County Animal Control, as he also undergoes a series of rabies shots. He had his second round of shots on Wednesday. Tucker has also spent time warning his neighbors about the situation. Christina Gulla, who lives in the neighborhood, said, "It's a little scary. I have kids. Gotta keep them inside, I guess." Although the shots are unpleasant, Tucker said he is thankful he is getting treated. He told Action News he will continue to keep his guard up as officials look for the second raccoon. "You live in nature, so you just gotta be aware of nature," Tucker said. "But, as I said, I was in my yard; you're not expecting something to come shooting out of the bushes." The Gloucester County Health Department is warning residents to avoid contact with wild animals and to keep pets up to date on their vaccinations. news.content_original: 24/7 LivePhiladelphiaPennsylvaniaNew JerseyDelaware 89° Raccoons 2nd raccoon sought after rabies-positive animal attacks South Jersey man By6abc Digital Staff and Caroline Goggin Thursday, July 30, 2026 3:35AM 2nd raccoon sought after rabies-positive animal attacks NJ man GLASSBORO, N.J. (WPVI) -- Gloucester County officials are searching for a raccoon after another animal involved in an encounter tested positive for rabies. The investigation stems from an attack Sunday morning outside the Glassboro home of Kevin Tucker. "I was walking to leave when a raccoon came out of the shrubbery and charged me," Tucker said. "I kind of fell backward, and I think that's when it bit the front part of my right leg." READ MORE | Man recalls raccoon attack outside NJ home: 'I could see these bright yellow eyes' The raccoon was eventually captured in Anthony Alvarado's backyard - just steps from where Tucker was bitten. "It was running around making weird noises," Alvarado told Action News. "It was actually kind of foaming at the mouth a bit, so that's how I knew it had rabies." Officials said the raccoon that attacked Tucker has since tested positive for rabies. Authorities also said the infected animal had been seen fighting with another raccoon before its capture. Efforts are now underway to locate that second raccoon. Action News returned to the neighborhood on Wednesday afternoon to speak with Tucker, who said he is now on high alert. "I just don't know what might pop out of where and when," he said. He has spent the past few days fielding phone calls from the Gloucester County Health Department and Gloucester County Animal Control, as he also undergoes a series of rabies shots. He had his second round of shots on Wednesday. Tucker has also spent time warning his neighbors about the situation. Christina Gulla, who lives in the neighborhood, said, "It's a little scary. I have kids. Gotta keep them inside, I guess." Although the shots are unpleasant, Tucker said he is thankful he is getting treated. He told Action News he will continue to keep his guard up as officials look for the second raccoon. "You live in nature, so you just gotta be aware of nature," Tucker said. "But, as I said, I was in my yard; you're not expecting something to come shooting out of the bushes." The Gloucester County Health Department is warning residents to avoid contact with wild animals and to keep pets up to date on their vaccinations. Anyone bitten or scratched by a wild animal should seek medical attention immediately and contact local animal control or health officials. Report a correction or typo Copyright © 2026 WPVI-TV. news.content: Saturday, August 187°F / Aspen, CO e-Edition News News Latest News Government Cops and Courts Arts & Entertainment Sports Business Business Business News Real Estate Transactions Opinion Letters to Editor A&E Calendar Calendar Calendar of Events Submit a Calendar Event Obituaries About Shop Donate e-Edition Main e-Edition NewsBusiness Opinion & Commentary Letters to Editor Arts & Entertainment Calendar Local Magazine Obituaries About Newsletters Classifieds Shop Donate About Contact Us Impact Report Ethics Policy Advertise ADN Story Studio Media Kit Social Instagram Facebook X News July 31, 2026 Several Hunter Creek residents get rabies vaccines after bat exposures No bats have tested positive, but officials recommend shots as preventive measure Lucy PetersonAspen Daily News Staff Writer Pitkin County officials are working to mitigate a bat infestation in Hunter Creek, capturing and testing some for rabies. No bats have tested positive, but some residents were required to get post-exposure rabies vaccinations. Courtesy of Lauren Wenzel-Martenson/Snowmass Village Animal Services Pitkin County officials are mitigating a bat infestation in Hunter Creek that has required several people to get post-exposure rabies vaccinations and displaced two residents. One unit in the Hunter Creek Condominiums had “concerning bat activity,” said Carlyn Porter, Pitkin County’s emergency response and epidemiology program administrator, after a hole in the roof had previously been sealed and trapped a bat colony inside. Six Hunter Creek residents have been recommended for a post-exposure prophylaxis rabies vaccine, according to a letter sent to residents by The Romero Group, the property manager. It is a series of shots over a few weeks after exposure. “Two different pest control companies are working on the process,” Porter said. “We also want to remind folks that it can be challenging to mitigate while the bats are roosting during their breeding season, so right now we’re seeing a lot of baby bats ... that are just learning how to fly, and that’s the main reason the bats are coming into human habitation is to roost and have their babies.” While the county is seeing a “potentially record-breaking year of rabies activity in terms of potential exposures,” Porter said, none of the recovered bats have tested positive for rabies. But, especially in cases of infestations, anyone who has been exposed to bats is recommended to receive the rabies vaccines to prevent infection. “Typically, [if] it’s one bat we can isolate, we can test,” Porter said. “When it’s an entire colony, it’s really a shot in the dark if you’re testing one bat, and there’s potentially 100 more, so we’re making more recommendations [for vaccines] than we would in a situation where it’s an isolated exposure.” Advertisement In Hunter Creek, “it’s been a building-wide risk assessment process where we’re going unit by unit and determining if there was any activity,” Porter said. Susan Capiel, who lives directly below the Hunter Creek unit that had the infestation, captured two bats in her unit and released them. She and her husband are currently receiving their rabies vaccines. They have been keeping their doors and windows closed — despite the heat — in order to avoid another bat encounter. “We’re going to have to put up with this until it gets cooler and the bats migrate,” Capiel said. “I’ve been just still closing the doors over the screens at night because I just don’t want to be sleeping and have something happen.” Keep up or miss out!Wake up to today's headlines in your inbox. Information is just a click away. Do not fill this field Sign Up Capiel and Porter both said the residents of the infested unit are moving out because of the infestation. The Romero Group is working with the county’s health department, two pest control companies and two cleaning companies to address the infestation and make sure the affected unit is habitable, according to the letter sent to residents and reviewed by the Aspen Daily News. The Romero Group will also cover all expenses for physical repairs to HOA property caused by the incident, cleaning and testing costs inside the affected unit and will reimburse any uninsured medical expenses for the six individuals in Hunter Creek who elected to undergo the rabies vaccination, according to the letter. Porter and Aspen Wildlife Coordinator Lara Xaiz said bedroom exposures are the highest risk, since people can’t be sure if a bat has scratched or bitten them in their sleep. They suggest isolating bats to one room by shutting doors and windows and placing a towel under the door so the bat can’t escape, before calling animal control. They also recommend trying to place a box or Tupperware container over a bat that is on the ground. A bat specialist is setting up an agitator in the infested unit to force the bats to leave and not return. They will then seal any entrances after the bats leave. As officials mitigate the bat colony, people may see bats around town or on the ground. While they may look lethargic or sick, Xaiz said they likely are not. Most of them are juvenile bats who struggle to fly when they are on the ground and are just not strong enough to fly yet, she said. “There is no indication that these bats are sick,” Xaiz said. She added that people should keep pets on a leash and not handle the bats themselves. “Never handle, never touch, keep your screens closed so they don’t come flying into your building or your home at night,” Xaiz said. lucy@aspendailynews.com Story Tags Health Advertisement Related News Aug. 1 Aspen Area Community Trust receives nonprofit status News Aug. 1 Cheerleading for democracy, McFaul draws packed house News Aug. 1 Local news in brief, Aug. 1 News July 31 Glenwood Canyon construction planned during 2027 airport clo... She added that people should keep pets on a leash and not handle the bats themselves. “Never handle, never touch, keep your screens closed so they don’t come flying into your building or your home at night,” Xaiz said. lucy@aspendailynews.com Story Tags Health Advertisement Related News Aug. 1 Aspen Area Community Trust receives nonprofit status News Aug. 1 Cheerleading for democracy, McFaul draws packed house News Aug. 1 Local news in brief, Aug. 1 News July 31 Glenwood Canyon construction planned during 2027 airport clo... Teenager swimming in Maryland lake bitten by rabid beaver Abigail Constantino | aconstantino@wtop.com July 27, 2026, 6:18 PM Share This: share on facebook share on X share on threads share on linkedin share on email print It happened Sunday around 9 a.m. as the teenager was in a designated swim area at Cunningham Falls State Park in Frederick County. A teenager who was swimming in a Maryland lake was bitten by a beaver that tested positive for the rabies virus. Related stories Health officials warn of potential rabies exposure in Loudoun County, elsewhere Rabies alert issued by Alexandria Health Department after fox tests positive Fox tests positive for rabies in Alexandria It happened Sunday around 9 a.m. as the teenager was in a designated swim area at Cunningham Falls State Park in Frederick County. Animal control picked up the beaver later that day from the Maryland Department of Natural Resources. On Monday, the Maryland Department of Health notified the Frederick County Health Department that the beaver tested positive for rabies. Authorities said swimming is prohibited in the William Houck Area in Hunting Creek Lake until it can be confirmed safe, which could take several days. “Mammals can be infected with the rabies virus, therefore do not touch or play with unknown animals. If you or your pets have contact with a wild animal contact the local authorities,” said Barry Glotfelty, director of the county’s Environmental Health Services. If you believe you had contact with this beaver or any other wildlife, call your doctor and the Frederick County Health Department’s Community Health Services Office at 301-600-3342. For pets or livestock, call your veterinarian and notify the county’s Environmental Health Office at 301-600-1717. Rabies is a viral disease that mainly infects mammals and is spread through the saliva of the infected animal, usually by a bite, the Frederick County Health Department said in a news release. “Symptoms of rabies in animals may include fear of water, excessive salivation, failure to eat or drink, limping, unusually friendly or aggressive behavior and/or other atypical behaviors such as nocturnal animals emerging during the daytime,” the health department said. The disease is nearly always fatal to humans if infected and no prompt post-exposure treatment is had. news.source_body_en: A teenager swimming in a Maryland lake was bitten by a beaver that later tested positive for rabies, prompting health officials to close a section of Cunningham Falls State Park. The incident occurred Sunday morning in a designated swim area at Hunting Creek Lake. Animal control retrieved the beaver, and the Maryland Department of Health confirmed the rabies diagnosis the following day. Authorities have prohibited swimming in the William Houck Area until it can be deemed safe, a process that may take several days. Health officials are urging anyone who had contact with the beaver or other wildlife to seek medical attention and contact the Frederick County Health Department. Rabies, a viral disease spread through animal bites, is nearly always fatal in humans without immediate treatment.

news.content_title: 2 Ohio counties confirm bats with rabies
news.content: COLUMBUS, Ohio — The Coshocton Public Health District and the Highland County Health Department confirmed Thursday that bats have tested positive for rabies. In Coshocton, one bat was confirmed with rabies in Franklin Township. The Highland County Health Department didn't state where the other bat was found. "Rabies is a serious disease, but there is no need for panic," said Kristina Bell, Coshocton Public Health Commissioner. "We want to remind our community to follow these steps, and seek medical help promptly if you have been exposed. Treatment for rabies is highly effective, if sought quickly." Those who believe they may have been exposed to rabies should seek immediate medical attention. Individuals will go through a process called post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) which includes wound care, human rabies immune globulin and a series of four or five rabies vaccines, which must be given as soon as possible after exposure, according to the department. The process is nearly 100% effective. If Ohioans find a bat in their homes, they're encouraged to take the following steps: - Close all windows and doors, and leave the bat in the room - Call a professional to capture the bat - If there is no professional to capture the bat, Miami County Public Health recommends putting on leather gloves, slowly approaching the bat when it lands, and placing a see-through container over the bat. Then, slide a lid under the container to trap the bat. Secure the lid with tape and punch small holes in the container to allow the bat to breathe As of June 8, there have been 15 confirmed rabies cases in Ohio and all from bats, according to the Ohio Department of Health. In mid-May, that number stood at seven. In 2025, there were 19 confirmed cases of bats with rabies across the state, a sharp decline from 2024, which had 43. In Ohio, there are more than 20,000 bite exposures and 1,000 non-bite exposures are reported in Ohio each year, exposing more than 21,000 people, according to ODH. Non-bite exposures can happen when a bat is found in a room with a child, someone who is sleeping or someone with a sensory or mental impairment

(WCIV) — More cases of rabies among animals were recorded in South Carolina, according to newly released information from the state's Department of Public Health. On Friday, the agency confirmed a raccoon near Wappoo Drive and Hinson Avenue in Charleston tested positive for rabies. One person was exposed and has been referred to their healthcare provider, state officials said. It marks the second rabid raccoon uncovered in less than two weeks. On Tuesday, July 21, a rabid raccoon was located in the area of Erica Road and Quarter Hoss Lane in Hollywood. Two people in that case were exposed. The second case came from a bat near North Main and West Court streets in Greenville. One person was also exposed there and referred to their healthcare provider for treatment. “Rabid bats have been known to transmit the rabies virus,” said Terri McCollister, the rabies program manager. “People don’t always realize they or a pet have been bitten since bat teeth are tiny and bites are easy to overlook.” READ MORE | "Rabid raccoon confirmed in Orangeburg County after dog exposure, DPH says." To safeguard against rabies exposure, the public is encouraged always to assume a person or a pet has potentially been bitten by a rabid bat when they wake up to find a bat in a room or tent; a bat is found where children, pets, or persons with impaired mental capacity (intoxicated or mentally disabled) have been left unattended; or they have been in direct contact with a bat. McCollister, however, stressed that not all bats are infected with rabies. “Although bats can carry rabies, not every bat is infected with the virus," McCollister said. "Bats are an important part of South Carolina's ecosystems and deserve a healthy degree of respect just like all wild animals." The health department stressed the need to keep pets up to date on rabies vaccinations as the easiest way to protect against the disease. In 2026, this bat is the fourth animal in Greenville County to test positive for rabies and the Charleston raccoon is the eighth animal to test positive for rabies in that county. 31, 2026 at 4:24 PM 3VIEW ALL PHOTOS FILE - A file image of a raccoon. (Photo credit: N.C. Wildlife Resources Commission) 0Comment Share topics: Rabies Raccoon Charleston South Carolina Wappoo Drive Hinson Avenue Greenville Bat CHARLESTON, S.C. (WCIV) — More cases of rabies among animals were recorded in South Carolina, according to newly released information from the state's Department of Public Health. On Friday, the agency confirmed a raccoon near Wappoo Drive and Hinson Avenue in Charleston tested positive for rabies. One person was exposed and has been referred to their healthcare provider, state officials said. It marks the second rabid raccoon uncovered in less than two weeks. On Tuesday, July 21, a rabid raccoon was located in the area of Erica Road and Quarter Hoss Lane in Hollywood. Two people in that case were exposed. The second case came from a bat near North Main and West Court streets in Greenville. One person was also exposed there and referred to their healthcare provider for treatment. “Rabid bats have been known to transmit the rabies virus,” said Terri McCollister, the rabies program manager. “People don’t always realize they or a pet have been bitten since bat teeth are tiny and bites are easy to overlook.” READ MORE | "Rabid raccoon confirmed in Orangeburg County after dog exposure, DPH says." To safeguard against rabies exposure, the public is encouraged always to assume a person or a pet has potentially been bitten by a rabid bat when they wake up to find a bat in a room or tent; a bat is found where children, pets, or persons with impaired mental capacity (intoxicated or mentally disabled) have been left unattended; or they have been in direct contact with a bat. McCollister, however, stressed that not all bats are infected with rabies. “Although bats can carry rabies, not every bat is infected with the virus," McCollister said. "Bats are an important part of South Carolina's ecosystems and deserve a healthy degree of respect just like all wild animals." The health department stressed the need to keep pets up to date on rabies vaccinations as the easiest way to protect against the disease. In 2026, this bat is the fourth animal in Greenville County to test positive for rabies and the Charleston raccoon is the eighth animal to test positive for rabies in that county. All rights reserved More Health: Health News Parenting Wellness Healthy Eating Mental Health Addiction Newsletters July 29, 2026 South Jersey man bitten by rabid raccoon; health officials advise people to avoid wild animals People are advised to seek immediate medical attention if they are scratched or bitten by an animal suspected of having rabies. By Courtenay Harris Bond PhillyVoice Staff Prevention Rabies from Jeffry Surianto/Pexels After a South Jersey man was bitten by rabid raccoon, Gloucester County officials advised people to avoid wild animals and take other precautions. The photo above is a stock image. Read More A raccoon that bit a South Jersey man on Sunday has tested positive for rabies. "I was walking to leave when a raccoon came out of the shrubbery and charged me," Kevin Tucker, of Glassboro, Gloucester County, told 6ABC on Tuesday. "I kind of fell backward, and I think that's when it bit the front part of my right leg." MORE: Penn bioethicist criticizes FDA panel's endorsement of six peptides On Wednesday, Gloucester County health officials warned people to avoid wild animals and keep their distance from stray dogs and cats. They also advised pet owners to ensure that their pets have been vaccinated against rabies. "Be aware that high risk wildlife such as raccoons, foxes and skunks also feed in areas where outside cats are fed," health officials warned. Anyone that sees an animal that is behaving strangely or acting disoriented is advised not to handle it and immediately call Gloucester County animal control at (856) 881-2828. What is rabies? Rabies is a viral disease that attacks the central nervous system and brain. It can be fatal if a person becomes symptomatic before getting medical attention. Rabies spreads through contact with the saliva of infected animals. Fewer than five people each year test positive for rabies, but many more people come into contact with rabid animals, according to Yale Medicine. Warm-blooded mammals are all susceptible to rabies, including raccoons, skunks, foxes, bats and dogs. Most dogs in the United States are vaccinated against rabies. Bats are the most common cause of the disease in the United States. Because of its strict quarantine laws, Hawaii is the only state that is free of rabies. When to get a rabies shot Rabies symptoms mimic flu symptoms, including fatigue, weakness, fever and headache, which can make diagnosis tricky. Signs of rabies may also include prickling, itching and discomfort where a person has been bitten. More advanced symptoms include hallucination, anxiety, agitation, extreme thirst and saliva production, and aggression and thrashing, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention says. It can be weeks or months after a bite from a rabid animal before the first symptoms of rabies appear – and about two weeks between early signs and extreme symptoms. But rabies is incurable and fatal once a person develops clinical symptoms, the CDC says. This is why it is crucial for people to seek immediate medical attention after being scratched or bitten by an animal that may be rabid. Clinicians at an emergency departments can determine whether a potentially exposed person needs a rabies shot. According to CDC guidelines, a person who has not been vaccinated against rabies should first receive a shot of human rabies immune globulin. This shot gives a person antibodies to fight off the virus until the subsequent vaccination takes hold. The rabies vaccine should be given at the first medical visit. Additional doses should be given three days later, seven days later and 14 days later. People with immune disorders may need a fifth shot, the CDC says. All rights reserved More Health: Health News Parenting Wellness Healthy Eating Mental Health Addiction Newsletters July 29, 2026 South Jersey man bitten by rabid raccoon; health officials advise people to avoid wild animals People are advised to seek immediate medical attention if they are scratched or bitten by an animal suspected of having rabies. By Courtenay Harris Bond PhillyVoice Staff Prevention Rabies from Jeffry Surianto/Pexels After a South Jersey man was bitten by rabid raccoon, Gloucester County officials advised people to avoid wild animals and take other precautions. The photo above is a stock image. Read More A raccoon that bit a South Jersey man on Sunday has tested positive for rabies. "I was walking to leave when a raccoon came out of the shrubbery and charged me," Kevin Tucker, of Glassboro, Gloucester County, told 6ABC on Tuesday. "I kind of fell backward, and I think that's when it bit the front part of my right leg." MORE: Penn bioethicist criticizes FDA panel's endorsement of six peptides On Wednesday, Gloucester County health officials warned people to avoid wild animals and keep their distance from stray dogs and cats. They also advised pet owners to ensure that their pets have been vaccinated against rabies. "Be aware that high risk wildlife such as raccoons, foxes and skunks also feed in areas where outside cats are fed," health officials warned. Anyone that sees an animal that is behaving strangely or acting disoriented is advised not to handle it and immediately call Gloucester County animal control at (856) 881-2828. What is rabies? Rabies is a viral disease that attacks the central nervous system and brain. It can be fatal if a person becomes symptomatic before getting medical attention. Rabies spreads through contact with the saliva of infected animals. Fewer than five people each year test positive for rabies, but many more people come into contact with rabid animals, according to Yale Medicine. Warm-blooded mammals are all susceptible to rabies, including raccoons, skunks, foxes, bats and dogs. Most dogs in the United States are vaccinated against rabies. Bats are the most common cause of the disease in the United States. Because of its strict quarantine laws, Hawaii is the only state that is free of rabies. When to get a rabies shot Rabies symptoms mimic flu symptoms, including fatigue, weakness, fever and headache, which can make diagnosis tricky. Signs of rabies may also include prickling, itching and discomfort where a person has been bitten. More advanced symptoms include hallucination, anxiety, agitation, extreme thirst and saliva production, and aggression and thrashing, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention says. It can be weeks or months after a bite from a rabid animal before the first symptoms of rabies appear – and about two weeks between early signs and extreme symptoms. But rabies is incurable and fatal once a person develops clinical symptoms, the CDC says. This is why it is crucial for people to seek immediate medical attention after being scratched or bitten by an animal that may be rabid. Clinicians at an emergency departments can determine whether a potentially exposed person needs a rabies shot. According to CDC guidelines, a person who has not been vaccinated against rabies should first receive a shot of human rabies immune globulin. This shot gives a person antibodies to fight off the virus until the subsequent vaccination takes hold. The rabies vaccine should be given at the first medical visit. Additional doses should be given three days later, seven days later and 14 days later. People with immune disorders may need a fifth shot, the CDC says. news.content: Fox 8 Cleveland WJW Bat tests positive for rabies in Coshocton County Kevin Accettulla 1 day ago COSHOCTON, Ohio (WCMH) — A bat tested positive for rabies in Coshocton County, local health officials said Thursday. The Coshocton Public Health District was notified of the positive test on Wednesday by the Ohio Department of Health. The positive test was from Franklin Township, which includes Franklin, Conesville and Wills Creek. No human exposures were confirmed, according to the district. Two animals that were directly exposed both had previously been vaccinated for rabies. Watch the latest headlines from NBC4 in the player above. There have been 16 bats in 14 counties that have tested positive for rabies in 2026. Rabies is a deadly virus that can affect any mammal, including pets and humans. It attacks the nervous system and can spread through saliva, often through bites. “Rabies is a serious disease, but there is no need for panic,” Public Health District Commissioner Kristina Bell said in a statement. The health district recommends the community avoid contact with wild animals or strays, don’t approach animals that appear sick, injured or dead, and ensure pets are up-to-date on their rabies vaccines. Robiller / Naturlichter.de / CC BY-SA 3.0 DE / MGN) By Aspen Andrews Published: Jul. 30, 2026 at 11:34 PM UTC Share Add Us On GoogleAdd as a preferred source on Google CUSTER COUNTY, Colo. (KKTV) -On Thursday afternoon, health officials said a bat found near Valley View Road in Custer County tested positive for rabies. Custer County Public Health Agency is asking the community to avoid contact with all wild and stray animals, including bats, during this time. According to health officials, what could seem to be insignificant contact with a bat could still be enough to transmit rabies. Rabies commonly spreads through contact with an infected animal’s saliva as a result of bites or exposure to cuts, but in some instances, people may not realize they were bitten and may not see the wound. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention shared several tips to help control and prevent rabies: Making sure your pets are up to date on their rabies vaccines Keeping wildlife wild - stay away from wildlife for both human and animal safety Calling animal control to remove stray animals from your neighborhood Washing bites or scratches immediately with soap and water after possible rabies exposure Seeking medical care urgently if you may have been exposed to rabies If you find a dead bat or one that seems to be behaving strangely, you are urged to contact Custer County Public Health Agency or Colorado Parks and Wildlife. If you believe the bat had contact with a human or pet, especially in an enclosed building, collect the bat without physical contact and bring it to Custer County Public Health Agency. Follow us on Google Wild boars gather in a residential area in the northern Israeli city of Haifa on December 5, 2019. (photo credit: Menahem Kahana/AFP via Getty Images) ByDANYA SAPERSTEIN JULY 28, 2026 12:08 Rabies cases have more than tripled in the past four years, spreading throughout the country, according to a Health Ministry statement released on Tuesday. The Health Ministry is “very concerned” over rabies, which has shown an “alarming increase” in wild animals, some of whom are encroaching on urban areas, including jackals in Tel Aviv and wild boars in Haifa. Rabies is a fatal disease endemic to Israel’s wild animal population. Once an animal or person is infected, without preventative treatment, the mortality rate is almost 100%. While preventative treatment has made human deaths from rabies in Israel rare, with only four after the state’s first decade, tens of thousands of people worldwide die from the disease each year. The disease attacks the central nervous system of mammals and is transmitted through bites or through contact between saliva and broken skin or mucous membranes. A bite, lick, or any other contact with the saliva of an infected animal can transmit the virus during a later stage of the disease, in most animals, within 10 days before their death. In recent years, rabies cases in Israel’s wild animal population have risen sharply, with a 252% increase between 2022 and 2025. In 2026, 69 animals have already been diagnosed, and the Health Ministry expects the number to reach around 150 by the end of the year. By comparison, this is up from 29 cases in 2022. A jackal is seen at Hayarkon Park in Tel Aviv, on September 03, 2022. (credit: TOMER NEUBERG/FLASH90) Human activity leads to geographic spread of infected animals The increase is partially due to the geographic spread of infected animals. Rabies can spread to a region through both animal movement and feeding practices. Intentionally leaving out food for stray cats may also feed other wild animals, as can leaving garbage in the street and poor sanitation. The Health Ministry warned that urban density, construction, and the displacement of wildlife from their natural habitats all contribute to the problem. Additionally, infected animals may be transported by people. In 2026, there were three such cases: a reservist who brought a dog from northern Israel to Hadera and Ra’anana, where it came into contact with his extended family over Passover, a dog who was brought from Ramallah to Holon, and an adopted dog that had never been vaccinated or examined by a veterinarian who traveled by train from Jerusalem to Tel Aviv, where it was brought to the beach. That incident ultimately required the Health Ministry to manage 52 exposure cases. The Health Ministry emphasized that in the event of an animal injury, one should first wash the affected area thoroughly with soap and water for about 10 minutes. They should then urgently contact their local health office to assess the level of risk and determine whether vaccination or other preventative treatment is necessary. No appointment is required for such a visit. When local health offices are closed, people should go to a hospital emergency department for initial treatment. (photo credit: Menahem Kahana/AFP via Getty Images) ByDANYA SAPERSTEIN JULY 28, 2026 12:08 Rabies cases have more than tripled in the past four years, spreading throughout the country, according to a Health Ministry statement released on Tuesday. The Health Ministry is “very concerned” over rabies, which has shown an “alarming increase” in wild animals, some of whom are encroaching on urban areas, including jackals in Tel Aviv and wild boars in Haifa. Rabies is a fatal disease endemic to Israel’s wild animal population. Once an animal or person is infected, without preventative treatment, the mortality rate is almost 100%. While preventative treatment has made human deaths from rabies in Israel rare, with only four after the state’s first decade, tens of thousands of people worldwide die from the disease each year. The disease attacks the central nervous system of mammals and is transmitted through bites or through contact between saliva and broken skin or mucous membranes. A bite, lick, or any other contact with the saliva of an infected animal can transmit the virus during a later stage of the disease, in most animals, within 10 days before their death. In recent years, rabies cases in Israel’s wild animal population have risen sharply, with a 252% increase between 2022 and 2025. In 2026, 69 animals have already been diagnosed, and the Health Ministry expects the number to reach around 150 by the end of the year. By comparison, this is up from 29 cases in 2022. A jackal is seen at Hayarkon Park in Tel Aviv, on September 03, 2022. (credit: TOMER NEUBERG/FLASH90) Human activity leads to geographic spread of infected animals The increase is partially due to the geographic spread of infected animals. Rabies can spread to a region through both animal movement and feeding practices. Intentionally leaving out food for stray cats may also feed other wild animals, as can leaving garbage in the street and poor sanitation. The Health Ministry warned that urban density, construction, and the displacement of wildlife from their natural habitats all contribute to the problem. Additionally, infected animals may be transported by people. In 2026, there were three such cases: a reservist who brought a dog from northern Israel to Hadera and Ra’anana, where it came into contact with his extended family over Passover, a dog who was brought from Ramallah to Holon, and an adopted dog that had never been vaccinated or examined by a veterinarian who traveled by train from Jerusalem to Tel Aviv, where it was brought to the beach. That incident ultimately required the Health Ministry to manage 52 exposure cases. The Health Ministry emphasized that in the event of an animal injury, one should first wash the affected area thoroughly with soap and water for about 10 minutes. They should then urgently contact their local health office to assess the level of risk and determine whether vaccination or other preventative treatment is necessary. No appointment is required for such a visit. When local health offices are closed, people should go to a hospital emergency department for initial treatment. analysis.time: Published on July 28, 2026. Event period spans from 2022 to 2026, with a notable increase in cases reported over the past four years.
analysis.location_and_population: Israel, specifically urban areas including Tel Aviv and Haifa, where wild animals such as jackals and wild boars are encroaching. The affected population includes both wild animals and humans exposed to potential rabies transmission.
analysis.event: Confirmed increase in rabies cases in Israel's wild animal population, with cases more than tripling over the past four years. The Health Ministry has expressed 'very concerned' status over the 'alarming increase' and the spread of rabies to urban areas.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: Rabies cases in wild animals rose by 252% between 2022 and 2025. In 2026, 69 animals have been diagnosed, with an expected total of around 150 by year-end, up from 29 cases in 2022. The disease is fatal with near 100% mortality rate without treatment, though human deaths in Israel are rare due to preventative measures. Risk includes potential human exposure through animal bites or saliva contact.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The Health Ministry is actively monitoring the situation and has issued public health guidelines, including wound washing procedures and urging contact with local health offices or emergency departments for potential exposures. The ministry is also investigating factors contributing to the spread, such as human feeding practices and wildlife displacement. No specific treatment or eradication plans are detailed in the evidence.

By 2026, 69 cases have been diagnosed, with projections reaching around 150 by year-end, up from just 29 in 2022. The alarming rise is attributed to wild animals like jackals and wild boars encroaching on urban areas such as Tel Aviv and Haifa, driven by human activity, construction, and wildlife displacement. Rabies, a fatal disease with near 100% mortality without treatment, is endemic in Israel's wild animal population and spreads through bites or saliva contact. The situation underscores growing public health risks as urbanization brings humans closer to infected wildlife.

USDA Conducts 2026 Oral Rabies Vaccination Efforts Targeting Wildlife in Eastern United States While rabies is almost always fatal once symptoms appear, it also is 100% preventable PUBLISHED ON July 31, 2026 USDA-APHIS Wildlife Services’ National Rabies Management Program distributes millions of oral rabies vaccine baits each year to help prevent the spread of this deadly disease in wildlife, such as raccoons, gray foxes, and striped skunks. (USDA photo by Wildlife Service, Public domain) WASHINGTON — The U.S. Department of Agriculture’s Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service (APHIS) will begin its annual distribution of RABORAL V-RG®, an oral rabies vaccine (ORV) bait, in select areas in the eastern United States to prevent the spread of raccoon rabies into America’s heartland. Rabies is a serious public health concern. While rabies is almost always fatal once symptoms appear, it also is 100% preventable. Human exposures can be successfully remedied if medical attention is sought immediately following exposure. Costs associated with rabies detection, prevention, and control may exceed $500 million annually in the United States. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), about 90 percent of reported rabies cases in the United States are in wildlife. APHIS and its cooperators will begin distributing ORV baits today across rural areas by airplane and in suburban or urban areas by helicopter, vehicle, and bait station. RABORAL V-RG® rabies baits are coated with a fishmeal attractant and are packaged in two-inch plastic sachets. The RABORAL V-RG® vaccine is safe for many animals, including domestic dogs and cats. Humans and pets cannot get rabies from contact with the baits but should leave them undisturbed if they are encountered. Dogs that consume many baits may experience a temporary upset stomach, but there are no long-term health risks. If people come in contact with baits, they should immediately wash the contact area with warm water and soap. ORV baits will be distributed during the following time periods and based out of airports in the cities listed below: In Northeast to Mid-Atlantic states during August: The Watertown, New York, project will include portions of northern New York in the St. Lawrence Valley region and distribute 220,000 baits by airplane, helicopter and vehicles. In addition to RABORAL V-RG®, APHIS will distribute another ORV bait, ONRAB, in select areas of New York as part of an ongoing field assessment. The Barre, Vermont, project will encompass parts of northern New Hampshire, northeastern New York and northern Vermont and distribute almost 460,000 baits by airplanes and vehicles. APHIS will also be distributing ONRAB in this region. The Houlton, Maine, project will cover parts of northern Maine and distribute approximately 598,000 ORV baits by airplane and vehicle. The Jamestown, New York, project will include areas in western New York and distribute approximately 379,000 ORV baits by airplane and helicopter. Field assessment of ONRAB will occur in this area concurrently. The North Lima, Ohio, project will involve distribution of approximately 729,000 RABORAL V-RG® baits in parts of western Pennsylvania. Field assessment of ONRAB will also occur in western Pennsylvania at the same time. The Buckhannon, West Virginia, project will include portions of western Pennsylvania and West Virginia, distributing approximately 364,000 ORV baits by airplane and vehicle. ONRAB field assessment also will take place in select areas of West Virginia. In Massachusetts from mid-September through mid-October: The Cape Cod, Mass., project will cover parts of peninsular and mainland Massachusetts and distribute 75,000 ORV baits by helicopter, bait station, and vehicle. In Southern states during October: The Abingdon, Va., project will cover parts of North Carolina, Tennessee, Virginia and a small portion of southern West Virginia, distributing more than 686,000 ORV baits by airplane, helicopter, and vehicle. The Andrews, N.C., project will include areas in western North Carolina and north Georgia and will distribute approximately 415,000 ORV baits by airplane, helicopter and vehicle. The Dalton, Ga., project will cover areas in Alabama, Georgia, North Carolina, and Tennessee, distributing 648,000 ORV baits by airplane and helicopter. The Gadsden, Ala., project will cover parts of northeast and central Alabama and distribute approximately 712,000 baits by airplane, helicopter, and vehicle. For additional information concerning rabies or the ORV program, please visit www.aphis.usda.gov/national-wildlife-programs/rabies or contact APHIS Wildlife Services toll free at 1-866-4-USDA-WS (1-866-487-3297). —USDA APHIS Spread the word Shares RECOMMENDED ARTICLES Removing Stigma & Building Mental Wellness in Farm Communities May 12, 2026 MAYVILLE, N.Y. — The next Rural Mental Health Connections Webinar, “Removing Stigma & Building Mental Wellness in Farm Communities,” will take place online May 28, 2026. USDA Conducts 2026 Oral Rabies Vaccination Efforts Targeting Wildlife in Eastern United States While rabies is almost always fatal once symptoms appear, it also is 100% preventable PUBLISHED ON July 31, 2026 USDA-APHIS Wildlife Services’ National Rabies Management Program distributes millions of oral rabies vaccine baits each year to help prevent the spread of this deadly disease in wildlife, such as raccoons, gray foxes, and striped skunks. (USDA photo by Wildlife Service, Public domain) WASHINGTON — The U.S. Department of Agriculture’s Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service (APHIS) will begin its annual distribution of RABORAL V-RG®, an oral rabies vaccine (ORV) bait, in select areas in the eastern United States to prevent the spread of raccoon rabies into America’s heartland. Rabies is a serious public health concern. While rabies is almost always fatal once symptoms appear, it also is 100% preventable. Human exposures can be successfully remedied if medical attention is sought immediately following exposure. Costs associated with rabies detection, prevention, and control may exceed $500 million annually in the United States. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), about 90 percent of reported rabies cases in the United States are in wildlife. APHIS and its cooperators will begin distributing ORV baits today across rural areas by airplane and in suburban or urban areas by helicopter, vehicle, and bait station. RABORAL V-RG® rabies baits are coated with a fishmeal attractant and are packaged in two-inch plastic sachets. The RABORAL V-RG® vaccine is safe for many animals, including domestic dogs and cats. Humans and pets cannot get rabies from contact with the baits but should leave them undisturbed if they are encountered. Dogs that consume many baits may experience a temporary upset stomach, but there are no long-term health risks. If people come in contact with baits, they should immediately wash the contact area with warm water and soap. ORV baits will be distributed during the following time periods and based out of airports in the cities listed below: In Northeast to Mid-Atlantic states during August: The Watertown, New York, project will include portions of northern New York in the St. Lawrence Valley region and distribute 220,000 baits by airplane, helicopter and vehicles. In addition to RABORAL V-RG®, APHIS will distribute another ORV bait, ONRAB, in select areas of New York as part of an ongoing field assessment. The Barre, Vermont, project will encompass parts of northern New Hampshire, northeastern New York and northern Vermont and distribute almost 460,000 baits by airplanes and vehicles. APHIS will also be distributing ONRAB in this region. The Houlton, Maine, project will cover parts of northern Maine and distribute approximately 598,000 ORV baits by airplane and vehicle. The Jamestown, New York, project will include areas in western New York and distribute approximately 379,000 ORV baits by airplane and helicopter. Field assessment of ONRAB will occur in this area concurrently. The North Lima, Ohio, project will involve distribution of approximately 729,000 RABORAL V-RG® baits in parts of western Pennsylvania. Field assessment of ONRAB will also occur in western Pennsylvania at the same time. The Buckhannon, West Virginia, project will include portions of western Pennsylvania and West Virginia, distributing approximately 364,000 ORV baits by airplane and vehicle. ONRAB field assessment also will take place in select areas of West Virginia. In Massachusetts from mid-September through mid-October: The Cape Cod, Mass., project will cover parts of peninsular and mainland Massachusetts and distribute 75,000 ORV baits by helicopter, bait station, and vehicle. In Southern states during October: The Abingdon, Va., project will cover parts of North Carolina, Tennessee, Virginia and a small portion of southern West Virginia, distributing more than 686,000 ORV baits by airplane, helicopter, and vehicle. The Andrews, N.C., project will include areas in western North Carolina and north Georgia and will distribute approximately 415,000 ORV baits by airplane, helicopter and vehicle. The Dalton, Ga., project will cover areas in Alabama, Georgia, North Carolina, and Tennessee, distributing 648,000 ORV baits by airplane and helicopter. The Gadsden, Ala., project will cover parts of northeast and central Alabama and distribute approximately 712,000 baits by airplane, helicopter, and vehicle. For additional information concerning rabies or the ORV program, please visit www.aphis.usda.gov/national-wildlife-programs/rabies or contact APHIS Wildlife Services toll free at 1-866-4-USDA-WS (1-866-487-3297). —USDA APHIS Spread the word Shares RECOMMENDED ARTICLES Removing Stigma & Building Mental Wellness in Farm Communities May 12, 2026 MAYVILLE, N.Y. — The next Rural Mental Health Connections Webinar, “Removing Stigma & Building Mental Wellness in Farm Communities,” will take place online May 28, 2026. news.content: News Sports Life & Events Real Estate Advertise Obituaries eNewspaper Legals COSHOCTON COUNTY Rabid bat confirmed in Coshocton County; no human exposure reported Leonard L. Hayhurst Coshocton Tribune July 31, 2026, 9:00 a.m. ET COSHOCTON − A bat in Franklin Township of Coshocton County has tested positive for rabies, but there was no confirmed exposure to humans. The Coshocton Public Health District said it was notified on July 29 of the positive test by the Ohio Department of Health, according to a community announcement. The announcement said animals that alerted the resident to the bat had direct exposure and were being monitored by local health officials. Both animals had received rabies vaccinations. According to the ODH, 15 additional bats in 14 counties have tested positive for rabies in 2026, including adjacent Tuscarawas and Muskingum counties. The disease attacks the nervous system, including the brain and spinal cord. Bats are the most common source of rabies exposure in Ohio, because bites are small and difficult to detect. It's also commonly found in raccoons and skunks. Rabies is transmitted via saliva through contact by a bite, open wound or mucus membrane in the eyes, nose and mouth. The health district recommends avoiding contact with wild or stray animals and never approach any sick, injured or dead animals. Residents should report any unusual animal behavior to local authorities and ensure pets are current on rabies vaccines. "Rabies is a serious disease, but there is no need for panic," Coshocton Public Health District Commissioner Kristina Bell said in the announcement. "We want to remind our community to follow these steps and seek medical help promptly if you have been exposed. news.content: Latest U.S. Iran War Ceuta Migrants World Politics Entertainment HealthWatch MoneyWatch Crime Space Sports Brand Studio The Free Press Local News Atlanta Baltimore Bay Area Boston Chicago Colorado Detroit Los Angeles Miami Minnesota New York Philadelphia Pittsburgh Sacramento Texas Live CBS News 24/7 Baltimore Bay Area Boston Chicago Colorado Detroit Los Angeles Miami Minnesota New York Philadelphia Pittsburgh Sacramento Texas 48 Hours 60 Minutes Shows 48 Hours 60 Minutes CBS Evening News CBS Mornings CBS Morning News CBS Reports CBS Saturday Morning The Daily Report The Dish Face the Nation Sunday Morning The Takeout Things That Matter The Uplift CBS News Investigates CBS News Confirmed Podcasts Newsletters Download Our App CBS News Team Executive Team Brand Studio Paramount+ Join Our Talent Community RSS Feeds Baltimore | News Weather Sports Video On WJZ 89° Local Maryland Best of WJZ at 9 Politics Consumer Business Health Entertainment First Alert Weather Radar & Maps Closings/Delays Weather Watchers All Sports CBS Sports HQ Ravens Orioles Terps College Sports Horse Racing Golf Odds WJZ at 9 Community MVP Volunteer with WJZ WJZ and the Baltimore Banner HealthyMD WJZ Investigates AFRAM Black History Month About Us Meet The Team Contact Us Share A News Tip Links & Numbers Nominate An MVP Advertise With Us Download The App Watch CBS News Local News Beaver tests positive for rabies after biting 13-year-old at Cunningham Falls State Park By Michelle Richardson Updated on: July 28, 2026 / 10:03 AM EDT / CBS Baltimore Add CBS News on Google A beaver that bit a 13-year-old boy Sunday at Cunningham Falls State Park has tested positive for rabies. According to the Department of Natural Resources, the incident occurred at the park's William Houck area near the North Beach of the lake at 9:10 a.m. on Sunday, July 26. The swimming beach was closed immediately while Maryland Park Services and Maryland Natural Resource Police searched for the Beaver so it could be tested for rabies. One beaver was found and tested positive for rabies, said a press release from the Frederick County Health Department. According to the Frederick County Health Department, the swimming area remains closed as of Monday, July 27, until the area is considered safe for visitors. Park staff are now working to determine whether any additional beavers are present. The 13-year-old sustained injuries to his hands and chest and was flown to Johns Hopkins Hospital for treatment. Frederick County Health Department encourages anyone who has had contact with this beaver or any other wild animal, should consult their health care provider and notify the FCHD's Community Health Services Office at 301-600-3342. For pets that have come into contact with wild animals, notify the FCHD's Environmental Health Office at 301-600-1717 or animal control at 301-600-1544. Barry Glotfelty, Director for FCHD's Environmental Health Services, advises, "Mammals can be infected with the rabies virus, therefore do not touch or play with unknown animals. If you or your pets have contact with a wild animal contact the local authorities For information on what to do if you have been bitten or scratched by an animal, visit Health.FrederickCountyMD.gov/RabiesExposure For more information on rabies, visit Health.FrederickCountyMD.gov/Rabies. Tech Rabid bat found in New Jersey attic leaves 3 cats exposed to rabies Once symptoms begin, the illness is almost always fatal. by Aaron GoldsteinAugust 1, 2026 share Facebook Twitter Link Copied! Photo Credit: iStock A rabid bat found in the attic of a New Jersey home is alarming residents, showing that even ordinary household spaces can become unexpected points of contact among people, pets, and wildlife. Officials thankfully said no people were exposed, but the household's three cats now face a weeks-long monitoring period after encountering the infected bat inside the home. What happened? According to reporting from The Philadelphia Inquirer, testing later showed that a bat removed from the attic of the Haddonfield home on April 18 had rabies. After it was taken from the house without incident, the animal was sent to Trenton for testing. "There were no human exposures. Three cats were exposed to the bat," the county health department said in a press notice. The department also explained that "Rabies is a serious illness, but it can be prevented by early treatment after exposure. If you have been bitten or scratched by a wild animal, it is important that you seek immediate medical attention." Rabies in animals remains a recurring issue across New Jersey, which recorded 174 cases last year and 26 more by the end of March this year, per the Inquirer. Human infections are much less common, with the last known rabies case contracted in the Garden State being reported in 1997. Why does it matter? Rabies is one of the most serious diseases that people and pets can contract from wildlife, even though human infections are uncommon. Once symptoms begin, the illness is almost always fatal. news.content_title: Two exposed after rabid raccoon, bat confirmed in South Carolina
news.content: Two exposed after rabid raccoon, bat confirmed in South Carolina Watch: 7.31 WYFF News 4 Morning Headlines 7.31 WYFF News 4 Morning Headlines WYFF US LIVE Current Time 0:00 / Total Duration 5:57 Sorry, this video is not available, please check back later. Advertisement Updated: 4:33 PM EDT Jul 31, 2026 Editorial Standards i Chloe McCoy Digital Content Producer Two exposed after rabid raccoon, bat confirmed in South Carolina Updated: 4:33 PM EDT Jul 31, 2026 Editorial Standards i Chloe McCoy Digital Content Producer GREENVILLE, S.C. — Two rabid animals have been confirmed in South Carolina, and health officials say two people have been exposed. According to the South Carolina Department of Health, a raccoon in Charleston County and a bat in Greenville County tested positive for rabies. Advertisement In Greenville, the bat was found near North Main and West Court Streets while the raccoon was found near Wappoo Drive and Hinson Avenue in Charleston. One person in each separate instance was exposed and referred to their healthcare provider for treatment. Officials ask that if you believe that you, someone you know, or your pets have been exposed to rabies contact SCDPH's Upstate Greenville-Spartanburg office at 864-372-3270 or the Charleston office at 843-953-4713 during normal business hours. SCDPH says as a reminder that you cannot tell if a bat, or any other animal, has rabies by simply looking at it as the disease must be confirmed in a laboratory. Unusual behavior in bats that might indicate the animal has rabies includes daytime activity, inability to fly, and being found in places they are not usually seen, like in your home or on your lawn. In 2026, this bat is the fourth animal in Greenville County to test positive for rabies and the Charleston raccoon is the seventh animal to test positive for rabies in that county. There have been 66 cases of rabid animals statewide this year, according to officials. Advertisement Updated: 4:33 PM EDT Jul 31, 2026 Editorial Standards i Chloe McCoy Digital Content Producer Two exposed after rabid raccoon, bat confirmed in South Carolina Updated: 4:33 PM EDT Jul 31, 2026 Editorial Standards i Chloe McCoy Digital Content Producer GREENVILLE, S.C. — Two rabid animals have been confirmed in South Carolina, and health officials say two people have been exposed. According to the South Carolina Department of Health, a raccoon in Charleston County and a bat in Greenville County tested positive for rabies. Advertisement In Greenville, the bat was found near North Main and West Court Streets while the raccoon was found near Wappoo Drive and Hinson Avenue in Charleston. One person in each separate instance was exposed and referred to their healthcare provider for treatment. Officials ask that if you believe that you, someone you know, or your pets have been exposed to rabies contact SCDPH's Upstate Greenville-Spartanburg office at 864-372-3270 or the Charleston office at 843-953-4713 during normal business hours. SCDPH says as a reminder that you cannot tell if a bat, or any other animal, has rabies by simply looking at it as the disease must be confirmed in a laboratory. Unusual behavior in bats that might indicate the animal has rabies includes daytime activity, inability to fly, and being found in places they are not usually seen, like in your home or on your lawn. In 2026, this bat is the fourth animal in Greenville County to test positive for rabies and the Charleston raccoon is the seventh animal to test positive for rabies in that county. There have been 66 cases of rabid animals statewide this year, according to officials.
