Subscribe Today Sign In Share this: Print (Opens in new window) Print Share Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Share on Nextdoor (Opens in new window) Nextdoor Share on Bluesky (Opens in new window) Bluesky Share on LinkedIn (Opens in new window) LinkedIn Share on X (Opens in new window) X Email a link to a friend (Opens in new window) Email The Maine Center for Disease Control and Prevention announced Wednesday that a handful of bats have tested positive for rabies so far this year. With midsummer marking the start of bats’ most active season in Maine (ending in early September), the agency shared precautions people should take should they be exposed to the flying mammals. How many bats have tested positive for rabies in Maine? As of July 17, the Maine CDC has tested 353 animals this year, just over half of them bats. Five bats have tested positive for rabies, the agency reported Wednesday, one in each of the following counties: Androscoggin, Cumberland, Kennebec, Penobscot and Somerset. In 2025, the Maine CDC tested 730 animals, more than 340 of them bats. Seven bats tested positive for rabies that year. The Maine Department of Health and Human Services has a rabies dashboard on its website with data on bats and other animals that have been tested. Advertisement About 4,000 animals in the United States test positive for rabies each year, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, roughly 35% of them bats. How common is rabies in humans? Human cases of rabies are extremely rare in Maine and the nation as a whole. One to three cases of human rabies are reported in the United States each year, according to the U.S. CDC. However, according to the federal agency, about 1.4 million people seek healthcare for potential rabies exposure in the United States each year. Maine has not reported a human case of rabies since 1937, according to the Maine CDC. Rabies can be prevented after exposure with post-exposure prophylaxis. About 100,000 Americans receive post-exposure prophylaxis each year, according to the CDC. How do animals spread rabies? Animals spread rabies through bites and sometimes scratches, according to the Maine CDC. It can also spread through contact with an infected mammal’s brain or spinal cord. Advertisement Rabies does not spread through blood, urine, feces, dried saliva or skunk spray, the Maine CDC said. When should I take precautions? The Maine CDC notes that it’s not always easy for someone to confirm whether they have come into contact with a bat, and not all infected animals show signs of rabies. Beyond bites and scratches, the agency says humans should be wary of exposure when they or others are incapacitated. That includes waking up and finding a bat in their room; or locating bats in the vicinity of those who may not be able to say whether they’ve come into contact, such as young children. It’s also recommended to keep a close eye on pets and livestock, and take precautions if they’ve been in a confined space with bats (like a room or barn) or you find a bat in their mouth. What should I do if I’ve been exposed to a bat? If you think a person or animal may have been exposed to a bat, the Maine CDC provides several steps to take. The first, if possible, is to safely capture the bat. If you can manage that, the next step is to contact the Maine Warden Service to get it tested for rabies. If a warden is not available, the Maine CDC suggests contacting your local Animal Control Officer to arrange a test. If you have been bitten or scratched by a bat, the Maine CDC advises washing the area with soap and warm water for 10 to 15 minutes and contacting a healthcare provider. For pets and livestock that have come into contact with a bat, the agency says to consult a veterinarian and always keep up to date on their rabies vaccinations. Tech Rabid groundhog underneath parked car attacks child in Pennsylvania The animal was found in poor health and later confirmed to be rabid. by Aaron GoldsteinAugust 1, 2026 share Facebook Twitter Link Copied! Photo Credit: iStock A rabid groundhog in Eastern Pennsylvania attacked a child on a residential street, prompting a warning from local police about the dangers of approaching wildlife that appears sick or aggressive. As human neighborhoods and wild animals' habitats increasingly overlap, even familiar backyard species can pose serious health risks. What happened? After the child was attacked in Nanticoke, police responded to the scene. The animal was found in poor health and later confirmed to be rabid, as WVIA reported. Thankfully, officers safely secured the animal and had it transported to the Pennsylvania Game Commission for testing. "A groundhog which was under a parked vehicle attacked a juvenile," the Nanticoke City Police Department wrote in a statement on Facebook. "... This groundhog was confirmed to be rabid. This post is to inform the public not to approach wild animals, and to protect your pets from them." Under state health guidance, a person is considered exposed to rabies if a rabid animal bites or scratches them. Chief of Police Michael Roke told WVIA that it appeared as if the child was bitten on the leg and scratched, though he added that he could not confirm this. Among diseases people can catch from wildlife, rabies is especially dangerous because survival is exceedingly rare once symptoms appear. State guidance cited by WVIA notes early symptoms can include fever, headache, fatigue, irritability, and pain or itching at the exposure site before the illness progresses to paralysis, seizures, delirium, and death. Warning signs for rabies in animals can include aggression, excessive drooling, vocalizations, lack of coordination, paralysis, and lack of fear around people. Pennsylvania typically confirms 350 to 500 rabid animals each year, according to WVIA. But human cases are far rarer. The most recent one reported dates all the way back to 1984. If you are bitten or scratched by a rabid animal or think you may have been exposed to one, contact a doctor immediately. The disease can be treated if caught quickly. Keep your distance from all wildlife, especially animals that behave oddly, whether that means they are disoriented, aggressive, or unafraid of humans. Those behaviors can signal illness, including rabies. Instead of intervening yourself, contact local authorities or wildlife officials, and make sure to keep pets and children out of harm's way. By Anisa Snipes Published: Jul. 31, 2026 at 6:45 PM UTC Share Add Us On GoogleAdd as a preferred source on Google GREENVILLE, S.C. (FOX Carolina) - The South Carolina Department of Public Health (DPH) confirmed one person was exposed to a rabid bat in downtown Greenville. Officials said the bat was found near North Main Street and West Court Street. It was submitted to DPH’s lab for testing on Wednesday and was confirmed to have rabies on Thursday. If you believe you or someone you know has come into contact with the bat, please call DPH’s Upstate Greenville-Spartanburg office at 864-372-3270. “Rabid bats have been known to transmit the rabies virus,” said Terri McCollister, Rabies Program manager. “People don’t always realize they or a pet have been bitten since bat teeth are tiny and bites are easy to overlook.” The DPH said you should always assume a person or pet has potentially been bitten when: They wake up to find a bat in a room or tent A bat is found where children, pets, or persons with impaired mental capacity (intoxicated or mentally disabled) have been left unattended They have been in direct contact with a bat Feel more informed, prepared, and connected with FOX Carolina. news.content_title: Oregon matches record-high number of bats infected with rabies
news.content: Oregon matches record-high number of bats infected with rabies Published 9:10 pm Thursday, July 30, 2026 Oregon health officials are urging people to prevent exposure to rabies as positive tests continue to creep toward a new record high. The Oregon Health Authority and the Oregon Department of Fish and Wildlife have had 22 bats test positive for rabies in 2026. That means the state has matched, and is poised to surpass, its record number of bats with rabies in a single year. Bats have carried the rabies virus within their populations for thousands of years and are known to be common carriers today — though generally at very low levels. Despite that, they account for the most human exposures to the virus of any other species in the United States. The highest number of animals testing positive for rabies since 2000 was in 2006. That year, 22 bats and 2 foxes were found to be carrying the disease. In 2023, 20 bats tested positive. “When people find a dead or dying bat, they may pick it up with their hands because they want to help it, or maybe they’re just curious,” said Emilio DeBess, public health veterinarian at OHA’s Public Health Division. “When a bat or other wild animal is sick or dying with rabies, there’s an increased chance they will bite or transmit the virus in other ways.” Bats and other wildlife rarely bite people, but may do so if they are sick or feel threatened. “Bats provide important ecosystem services in Oregon, but also globally with insect control, seed dispersal, and pollination of specific plants, supporting agriculture and forest systems,” said Colin Gillin, ODFW state wildlife veterinarian. “And like many animals that can carry disease, bats can also prevent or suppress disease by reducing mosquitoes and other vectors that carry human and animal pathogens.” What to do if you find a bat Bats are protected wildlife, which makes it illegal to harm or keep them. If you see a bat that appears to be sick: • Stay calm, do not touch it, and keep people and pets away. • When the sick or dead bat is indoors, do not release it. If safe to do so, place a container or box over the bat. • When the sick or dead bat is outdoors, cover it with a box or bucket to keep it in place if safe to do so. Finding a dead bat does not require action unless someone was bitten or scratched. • Contact your local health authority or a veterinarian if you believe you were exposed. • If multiple sick or dead bats are in an area, report it to the ODFW: https://tinyurl.com/4h6v8kdr • When a person or pet has been bitten or scratched by an animal that may have rabies, report the exposure immediately and seek medical care. • Make sure your dogs and cats’ vaccinations are up to date. • Protect your home from bats by covering vents, chimneys and other entry points with screens. Rabies Rabies is a viral disease that is deadly if people don’t receive medical care before symptoms start. It spreads through bites or scratches from an infected animal. The most commonly infected species are bats, skunks, raccoons and foxes. If you believe you were exposed to rabies, do not wait. Urgently seek medical attention. You will need a series of four to five rabies vaccinations, which must start as soon as possible. The disease is rare in people in the U.S., with fewer than 10 deaths reported each year. Initial symptoms include a flu-like illness and discomfort at the bite site. Severe symptoms appear within two weeks. They include anxiety, confusion, agitation, hallucinations, thirst, but panic about fluids, lots of saliva, and aggressive behavior. Learn more from the Centers for Disease Control: cdc.gov/rabies/about/index.html

Rabies Rabies is a viral disease that is deadly if people don’t receive medical care before symptoms start. It spreads through bites or scratches from an infected animal. The most commonly infected species are bats, skunks, raccoons and foxes. If you believe you were exposed to rabies, do not wait. Urgently seek medical attention. You will need a series of four to five rabies vaccinations, which must start as soon as possible. The disease is rare in people in the U.S., with fewer than 10 deaths reported each year. Initial symptoms include a flu-like illness and discomfort at the bite site. Severe symptoms appear within two weeks. They include anxiety, confusion, agitation, hallucinations, thirst, but panic about fluids, lots of saliva, and aggressive behavior. Learn more from the Centers for Disease Control: cdc.gov/rabies/about/index.html

news.content: Home & Garden Residents Urged Not To Touch Bats As 2 Bats Test Positive For Rabies DuPage County Two bats have tested positive for rabies in DuPage County so far this year, according to county health officials. Lisa Marie Farver , Patch Staff Posted Fri, Jul 31, 2026 at 12:17 am CT DUPAGE COUNTY, IL — "Never touch a bat," DuPage County Health Department (DCHD) cautions after two bats have tested positive for rabies in the county so far this year. In total, 82 people in the county have been treated for possible exposure to rabies in 2026. According to the Illinois Department of Public Health (IDPH), there are 13 different species of bats in Illinois. Most often, residents are likely to encounter little and big brown bats, silver-haired bats and eastern red bats. The Illinois State Veterinary Medical Association reports that between 93 and 97 percent of bats will test negative for the rabies virus. Nonetheless, they advise that a bat should be considered rabid until a test has proven otherwise. Find out what's happening in Wheaton for free with the latest updates from Patch. DCHD reports that bats are the primary source of rabies in Illinois. Bats who have been infected with rabies may: Find out what's happening in Wheaton for free with the latest updates from Patch. Be seen during the day (bats are active at twilight or after dark) Be found in unlikely places, including on lawns or inside homes Be unable to fly DCHD recommends the following to prevent contracting rabies from bats. Secure your home to prevent bats from getting in Avoid handling any bats in your home Contact animal control for help containing or removing bats Do not remove a bat until you have spoken with animal control Vaccinate pets for rabies Residents are advised to seek medical attention immediately if they have been bitten by a bat. Pets should be taken to a veterinarian immediately if they may have been exposed to rabies. Get more local news delivered straight to your inbox. Sign up for free Patch newsletters and alerts

news.title_original: Rabid bat found near North Main Street in Greenville; 1 exposed - greenvillejournal.com

analysis.time: Published on July 31, 2026; event date not specified but reported on the same day.
analysis.location_and_population: Greenville County, near North Main Street in Greenville; 1 exposed individual.
analysis.event: A rabid bat was found near North Main Street in Greenville, with 1 person exposed to the bat. This is the fourth animal to test positive for rabies in Greenville County so far this year, according to the Department of Public Health (DPH).
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: 1 exposed individual; no cases or deaths reported. The bat is the fourth rabid animal in Greenville County this year, indicating ongoing rabies activity in the area.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The DPH confirmed the rabies test result. No further details on investigation, testing, or treatment of the exposed individual were reported in the supplied evidence.

analysis.brief_en: On July 31, 2026, a rabid bat was discovered near North Main Street in Greenville, resulting in one human exposure. This marks the fourth animal to test positive for rabies in Greenville County this year, as confirmed by the Department of Public Health (DPH). While no cases or deaths have been reported, the incident highlights ongoing rabies activity in the area. Public health officials have not provided additional details regarding the investigation or the status of the exposed individual.

Never touch a bat: What you need to know about bats and rabies July 30, 2026.Reading time 9 minutes. Any person or animal that touched or had contact with the bat or its saliva could be at risk of getting rabies. If you see a bat, don’t touch it! Bats lying on the ground, flying during daytime, making a lot of noise, or otherwise acting sick are more likely to have rabies. Read More Rabid bat found in Renton at Gene Coulon Park July 29, 2026.Reading time 7 minutes. Anyone who might have had physical contact with this bat (even if not bitten) could be at risk and should seek medical evaluation immediately or call Public Health to determine if rabies preventative treatment is necessary. Read More Bridging the gap between incarceration and community life: Portraits of Public Health July 21, 2026.Reading time 5 minutes. A disproportionate number of people in jails and prisons have chronic medical or behavioral health conditions. When people leave jail, it’s a unique moment to connect them to services in the community that they may not have known about before. Maliha, a social worker in the Jail Health Release Program, shares about what she does to help people with a range of health conditions as they transition out of incarceration. Read More Rabid bat found in Seattle near the University of Washington July 17, 2026.Reading time 6 minutes. A rabid bat was found in Seattle on July 15, 2026, on the sidewalk on University Way Northeast, between NE 41st and NE 42nd streets. This is near Parrington Lawn, on the University of Washington campus, and is a busy area with many businesses. Anyone who might have had physical contact with this bat (even if not bitten) could be at risk and should seek medical evaluation immediately or call Public Health at 206-296-4774 to determine if rabies preventative treatment is necessary. Read More Explosive diarrhea sounds...rough. Any rumbling in King County? July 16, 2026.Reading time 8 minutes. A national outbreak of Cyclospora—more commonly known by its main symptom, explosive diarrhea–continues to grow, but here in King County, we have not seen any unexpected increases in cyclosporiasis (the disease caused by Cyclospora) so far. We talked with Ann Shen, the lead for foodborne and enteric disease investigations for Public Health – Seattle & King County, about the local situation. Beau, one of our septic experts, shares his passion for the importance of septic systems in protecting public health, safeguarding the environment, and allowing a property to function as a home. supplementary_news.content_title: Oregon matches record for bats testing positive with rabies
supplementary_news.content: News Sports Politics Outdoors Real Estate Advertise Obituaries eNewspaper Legals OREGON Oregon matches record for bats testing positive with rabies Makenzie Stamets Salem Statesman Journal Aug. 1, 2026, 4:02 a.m. PT After 22 Oregon bats have tested positive for rabies in 2026, Oregon Health Authority and the Oregon Department of Fish and Wildlife are reminding people how to prevent exposure risk. The primary way people can stay safe is to not touch dead or dying animals, officials said. Also, to keep pets away. Oregon has matched its record for bats that tested positive for rabies in a year, OHA said. Bats are the primary animal to expose humans to the virus in the U.S. Though people might want to help a dead or dying bat, more contact with bats increased rabies exposure risk, OHA’s Public Health Division veterinarian Emilio DeBess said. “When a bat or other wild animal is sick or dying with rabies, there’s an increased chance they will bite or transmit the virus in other ways," DeBess said. Bats and other wildlife rarely bite people, but might if they are sick or threatened, ODFW state wildlife veterinarian Colin Gillin said. "Bats provide important ecosystem services in Oregon, but also globally with insect control, seed dispersal, and pollination of specific plants, supporting agriculture and forest systems,” Gillin said. “And like many animals that can carry disease, bats can also prevent or suppress disease by reducing mosquitoes and other vectors that carry human and animal pathogens.” What to do if you come across a bat Since bats are protected wildlife, and it is illegal to harm or keep them. ODFW and OHA provided the following list of tips if you see a sick bat: Stay calm, do not touch it. Keep people and pets away. If the sick or dead bat is indoors, do not release it. It may have exposed someone or a pet to rabies. Place a container or box over the bat if it's safe. If the sick or dead bat is outdoors and may have exposed someone to rabies, cover it with a box or bucket to keep it in place. But, leave the bat alone unless someone was bitten or scratched before it died. Immediately report if a person or pet has been bitten or scratched by an animal that may have rabies to local animal regulation services or local public health authority. Seek medical care immediately from a medical provider or veterinarian. If multiple sick or dead bats are observed in an area report to ODFW. Avoid bats seen in the wild, such as while hiking. Teach children to avoid all contact with bats and other wildlife. Update dog or cat vaccinations, whether they are indoor or outdoor pets. Unvaccinated pets that come into contact with a bat may be quarantined for up to four months, or euthanized. Protect your home from bats by covering vents, chimneys, and other entry points with screens. If roosting bats are living in the attic, call a wildlife control operator, not ODFW. More information about rabies and bats is avaliable at OHA’s bats and rabies website and ODFW’s bats website. Makenzie Stamets is an outdoor intern at the Statesman Journal.
